title: Distributed SQL architecture and what Oracle didn't grasp about it
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
It's impressive to see how Spanner innovated with its database architecture, especially when many traditional database vendors still struggle to understand it even after ten years. Some database service providers believe they can achieve Distributed SQL by inserting a sharding coordinator between the application and multiple monolithic database instances. However, they fail to recognize that doing so means sacrificing crucial SQL features like global primary keys, unique constraints, referential integrity, and the relational rule that SQL applications should be independent of the physical organization of data.

On March 4, 2024, Oracle promoted its sharding feature to Globally Distributed Autonomous Database. This allows for comprehensive partitioning capabilities to be extended across multiple database nodes, similar to what IBM DB2 did long ago while Oracle advocated against shared-nothing databases. However, during the announcement, Oracle exposed a lack of knowledge about the Distributed SQL solutions they think they are competing with. They may believe that Distributed SQL is a kind of NoSQL, which deserves a better explanation of the architecture of Distributed SQL databases.

This was the slide from this announcement:

The YugabyteDB's logo is the right one, but CockroachDB's is outdated. TiDB, one of the four Distributed SQL database based on Spanner architecture, was completely ignored. That already says a lot about their research in this area. Or it could be on purpose, as they later pretended that Distributed SQL could not do analytics, so they ignored the one with a column store dedicated to analytics.

Google built Spanner for use cases where NoSQL wasn't enough. It doesn't run on top of NoSQL engines. It runs in place of it on top of distributed storage (Colossus for Spanner). The difference between Distributed SQL (like Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB) and Database Sharding (like Vitess, Citus, Aurora, Oracle) is full SQL support.

1. Distributed Database classification: NoSQL, NewSQL, DistSQL

Let's examine a relational database's most essential SQL features: defining primary keys, unique constraints, and foreign keys for referential integrity, and see how they are supported in NoSQL, NewSQL, and DistSQL.

🥉 NoSQL databases (Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB)

To scale horizontally, NoSQL has eliminated all SQL features. This means that the primary key must include the partition key, foreign keys, and joins are not supported, and secondary indexes are either local (with the same partition key as the table) or eventually consistent. The data model is hierarchical and governed by the partition key.

🥈 Sharded databases (Vitess, Citus, Aurora, Oracle Globally Distributed Database)

Sharded Databases are used to scale relational data horizontally. However, they allow all SQL features only for a single shard. Creating a global index, enforcing uniqueness across shards, and having foreign keys referencing a primary key in another shard is impossible. The application must design a hierarchical data model to work around this limitation where relational features are possible only under a single sharding key.

🥇 Distributed SQL (Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB)

To make distribution transparent to the application, it is beneficial to present the distributed database as a single global database. This is where Distributed SQL redesigns the database architecture instead of adding a layer on top of monolithic databases. The key-value granularity is used to distribute, replicate, and store table rows and index entries rather than traditional pages or blocks. This enables automatic sharding and load re-balancing when nodes are added or removed, a must for cloud-native databases.

I explained the architectural difference between Data Sharding and Distributed SQL in "Distributed Things" PostgreSQL. Let's explain what the engine SQL databases run on top of.

2. All SQL Processing is running on top of Storage layers

SQL is the API end-users or applications use to interact with the database. It is not a storage engine by itself. RDBMS can use different engines, and most of them have logical layers:

  • The SQL Processing layer transforms user queries to read and write operations for table rows, index entries, and transaction intents. In YugabyteDB, this is the "Languages and Relational Technologies (LRT)" with YSQL (the PostgreSQL compatible API) or YCQL (the Cassandra-like API).
  • The Storage layer applies those operations to the persistent storage, locally or distributed through network operations. In YugabyteDB, the "Distributed Storage and Transactions (DST)" is called DocDB as the internal API between the two layers is a document protobuf.

Some databases, like YugabyteDB, clearly separate layers, allowing multiple query APIs. MySQL also provides for various storage engines, such as InnoDB or MyRocks. On the other hand, some databases may be monolithic, but you can still see the layers in the stack trace. For instance, when Oracle Database reads a single row from a SQL table, the C functions involved become apparent on a strace -k :

You can decipher the names mentioned in http://orafun.info/ and observe that SQL processing always runs on top of the storage engine, as in all databases. In this example, OPI is the highest-level Oracle Program Interface (the wire protocol), QER is the Query Execute Rowsource (the SQL processing), and KDST is the Kernel Data Scan Table (the storage engine). In the storage layer and below, there is no SQL, but instead, blocks, rows, columns, and metadata in a proprietary format. However, claiming that Oracle operates on top of NoSQL would be incorrect. This is an internal implementation invisible to the user.

In all SQL databases, SQL is on top. When you drill down through the software layers, the relational tables exposed to the users become bits in blocks stored on disks. In the end, you find a storage engine that has nothing to do with SQL or NoSQL, it can be proprietary or open-source: Oracle Autonomous Database runs on top of Oracle ASM, Spanner runs on top of Colossus, and YugabyteDB on top of Linux filesystems for the freedom of running on any platform.

3. Key-value documents, Raft log, and LSM-Tree to distribute

The confusion may come from the fact that Distributed SQL databases use an intermediate key-value structure between the logical SQL tables and the physical block/page to store on disk. There are two main reasons.

The first reason is distributing and replicating the table rows, index entries, and transaction intents. To add no constraint on the application, this must operate at the lowest level, like the primary key for the table rows or the index key for the index entries. Those fit perfectly a key-value documents protocol. The distribution and replication of blocks are possible but more problematic (Oracle RAC hot blocks on B-Tree indexes are an example). Oracle also stores and replicates changes in sequential redo records. YugabyteDB indexes them with their key. Those are implementation details not related to the SQL API above.

The second reason is optimizing for modern storage. Traditional databases work on pages or blocks because that was the unit used to access the mechanical disks (HDD). Those disks have a per-block latency penalty. The B-Tree structure of indexes is commonly used to limit the latency for random reads. They are maintained with expensive random writes, but this is acceptable when most of them are in local memory buffers. However, this buffer pool cannot be shared efficiently through the network in a distributed database over zones or regions. With Modern storage (SDD), LSM-Tree indexes are preferred because their Log Structure transforms random writes (still expensive on SSD) into sequential writes (during flush and compaction). The Merge involves random reads, but those are fast on SSD.

YugabyteDB implements those LSM trees based on RocksDB. Of course, RocksDB is not an SQL database, like an Oracle datafile is not an SQL datastore, but both serve the SQL database by storing its data and transaction intents as blocks or documents. Nobody will call that "running on top of NoSQL engines". A NoSQL engine has no SQL layer on top of it, making it NoSQL.

4. How do you know if you run on a Distributed SQL database?

Beyond the limitations on global indexes and referential integrity, the distribution of transactions distinguishes Data Sharding and Distributed SQL. To be ACID, databases must store, atomically, the transaction status visible by all other transactions.

  • Each shard has a local transaction table in sharded databases like Oracle, Citus, or Aurora Limitless and needs to be synchronized by a coordinator.
  • In Distributed SQL, like YugabyteDB, the transaction table is distributed. It makes it resilient: the transaction continues over failures.

If you don't know if you are using a Database Sharding or Distributed SQL, there's a simple way to find it:

  • Database sharding occurs when the application must know a sharding key, similar to the NoSQL partition key. The application must be rerouted to a single shard to use all SQL features efficiently. Cross-shard transactions are possible, identical to XA, Database Links or Foreign Data Wrappers, but not with all SQL features.
  • If the application can ignore how data is distributed through the nodes, you use a Distributed SQL database and have all SQL features without limitations. The application connects to any node and sees one logical SQL database.

In a Distributed SQL database, the execution plan doesn't show individual shards or partitions because they can move transparently to rebalance the load without invalidating the plan. Here is an example on YugabyteDB: 

yugabyte=# create table demo as select generate_series(1,1000000);
SELECT 1000000

yugabyte=# explain
           select count(*) from demo
;
                          QUERY PLAN
---------------------------------------------------------------
 Finalize Aggregate  
   ->  Seq Scan on demo  
         Partial Aggregate: true

yugabyte=# explain (analyze, dist, debug, costs off, summary off)
           select count(*) from demo
;
                              QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------------------
 Finalize Aggregate (actual time=131.946..131.946 rows=1 loops=1)
   ->  Seq Scan on demo (actual time=131.931..131.935 rows=3 loops=1)
         Storage Table Read Requests: 1
         Storage Table Read Execution Time: 131.881 ms
         Metric rocksdb_number_db_seek: 3.000
         Metric rocksdb_number_db_next: 1000000.000
         Metric rocksdb_number_db_seek_found: 3.000
         Metric rocksdb_number_db_next_found: 999997.000
         Metric rocksdb_iter_bytes_read: 69705380.000
         Metric docdb_keys_found: 1000000.000
         Metric ql_read_latency: sum: 381198.000, count: 3.000
         Partial Aggregate: true

The execution plan queries a single table. From the execution statistics (explain analyze), there is a clue that the million rows are distributed into 3 servers because the partial aggregate counts 3 rows (for each partial count), but the execution plan scans one global SQL table.

If you think about the "run on top of NoSQL engine" slide: Which NoSQL engine returns partial counts that are all consistent as of a consistent point in time? Oracle didn't understand the Spanner architecture. NoSQL databases are eventually consistent but Distributed SQL databases are fully ACID.

5. The query layer is stateless to scale-out SQL processing

There is another good reason to have two layers, with SQL Processing on top of distributed Storage, and Transaction in a Distributed SQL database. SQL processing is stateless and can run on all nodes. This is why using PostgreSQL code in YugabyteDB doesn't inherit from the monolithic database limitations: only the stateless part is used. The complex SQL structures can scale out because this stateless structure processes them.

The stateful part can scale out because it uses simple key-value reads and writes, distributed in Raft groups and stored by RocksDB LSM-Tree. Monolithic databases have a single process receiving the queries, processing the SQL, and writing into the blocks and that's why they cannot use a Distributed SQL architecture but have to shard over monolithic databases.

That said, except for the message about running "on top of NoSQL engine", Oracle Sharding in the "Autonomous" Oracle managed service is great for its purpose like Data Sovereignty and to Partition to datacenters beyond the distances acceptable by Oracle RAC. It has many sharding methods that I described in Oracle Sharding methods compared to YugabyteDB. YugabyteDB does that with PostgreSQL partitioning, in the SQL layer, above the automatic distribution and replication of Distributed SQL used for resilience and elasticity.
